The Fort William branch of the Great War Veterans Association joins with the Dominion command in demanding from Pension Board immediate statement as to whether it intends to review claims now pending in accordance with Royal Commission findings. Board's refusal to act causing unwarranted distress and hardship among many widows, dependents, and disabled ex-service men throughout the Dominion. Urgently request immediate acceptance.
In view of the report of the royal commission, which has pointed out many defects in the carrying out of this act, I should like to ask: Does the hon. minister feel it within his power to instruct the Board of Pension Commissioners to cam' out the. intent of the law, as brought before the House of Commons last year by the parliamentary committee, and as explained to the House? speakeroldname: Hon. H. S. BELAND (Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment):
speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
It has come to my knowledge that a very large number of telegrams have been received by members of the House, and also by members of the government. As to the interpretation of the Pension Act by the Board of Pension Commissioners, my hon. friend and hon. members of this House are aware that it is entirely within

The Budget-Mr. Fielding

the discretion of that board. The question of the advisability of amending the Pension Act is for this House and parliament generally to consider. It is the intention of the government to bring down legislation during the present session with a view to remedying the grievances which have been uttered more or less all over Canada by the ex-service men. It is hoped that these amendments will meet the situation. Again repeating myself, I say that, as far as an interpretation of the act is concerned, it is entirely within the power and authority of the Board of Pension Commissioners.

The Board of Pension Commissioners, according to the ruling of the commission-I do not wish to discuss it, and I shall not do so except to say one wordhaving put up certain information to the minister for interpretation, and having finally taken their own interpretation, perhaps not according to what the minister had said, point out that these clauses should be interpreted to a certain extent with different points in view. Under the circumstances, does the minister not think that he might direct the Board of Pension Commissioners to interpret the act in the most broad-minded way possible, and will not he promise the House to bring down the alterations which he suggests at a very early date?

I propose to introduce in the House as soon as possible-as soon as the budget debate is* over. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY HON. W S. FIELDING, MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The financial affairs for
the fiscal year, 1921-1922, which was the last year of which we have the public accounts, call now for only a passing notice. With regard to that year, the year ended 31st March, 1922, it is worth while remembering that while the present government were in power at the time the accounts were made up at the close of the year, they had only been in power three months, and, therefore, it will not be unfair to treat that year as a Conservative year, inasmuch as the Conservative government of the day, in the discharge of their duties, prepared the estimates and voted the money, made the contracts, and practically controlled the expenditure of the year. So that I think we may count that year, practically speaking, as a Conservative year. I am going to ask at this stage, and at one of the other stages during my remarks, that the courtesy of the House be extended to me, which is usual, to enable me to put into Hansard, in the form of a summary some figures which I may present.
Income and Expenditure
The revenue for the year was $381,952,386.99 against ordinary expenditure of $347,560,690.63.

The Budget-Mr. Fielding
If the surplus is to be ascertained by comparing the ordinary revenue with the ordinary expenditure-and that was the time-honoured way of determining surpluses-then on that year there was a surplus of $34,391,696.36. But there was a capital expenditure of $16,295,332.55. If we take that into account, both ordinary expenditure and capital expenditure, there was still a surplus of $18,096,363.81. Then there were certain special expenditures, including demobilization charges, of $1,526,583.22. So, if we take into account ordinary expenditure, capital expenditure and what is called special expenditure, there still was a surplus of $16,569,780.59. So far this is a story of surpluses; but there is a further statement to be made which quite destroys that happy picture. There were charges for advances to railways of $97,950,645.36. If we take, then, the whole expenditure for the year, ordinary, capital, special and railways, there was a deficit in that year of $81,380,864.77. After allowances for some deductions are made, the net result was that in that year we added to the public debt $81,256,818.04.
We turn now to the year 1922-1923 which closed not many days ago. AVe have not the complete accounts before us, but there is sufficient information to enable us practically to announce the result. Ordinary revenue amounted to $393,619,000. These are estimates, as the figures are not absolutely final. Ordinary expenditure amounted to about $331,780,000. As between those two items, there was then a surplus of $61,839,000. Capital expenditure, however, represents $14,500,000; adjustment of war claims, $6,700,000; cost of loan flotations, $3,050,000; these representing in all $24,250,000. There was thus a surplus over ordinary, capital and special expenditures, of $37,589,000. But again the railways have to be taken into account. We had to advance during that year $92,190,000 for railways, and $6,060,720 for the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, making in all for that charge, $98,250,720. This, of course, takes up all the surplus I have mentioned and leaves a large balance on the other side of the account. If we take everything into consideration for the year, the net result was that . we added to the public debt in the year just closed $49,293,086. The receipt of something over $8,000,000 from the British government on exchange account helped us to keep down what otherwise would have been a larger addition to the public debt.
The Public Debt
The addition of nearly $50,000,000 to our public debt in the past year is not a situation that should cause very much satisfaction in
168J
any quarter. During the war it was inevitable that there should be large additions to the public debt, and after the war was over there also had to be large additions to the public debt; but the war has been over for several years; we are now getting to a period of peace, so-called, and many will think it is about time that we endeavoured to balance our budget; that is to say, that we no longer have the excuse of the war for spending more money than we receive. I suppose stern economists will say that that is what should be done. I confess, as Minister of Finance, that it would be very agreeable to me if I could present such a statement, and the temptation is strong to pile on the taxes and meet the difficulty. Many people who have the critical spirit, without responsibility, will probably say that that is what a Minister of Finance should do. There is, however, another side to the account. The people of Canada are pretty heavily taxed to-day; between Dominion, provincial and municipal taxation, the burdens of the people are very great, and I am reluctant to add to those burdens now by introducing new forms of taxation. Readjustments there will be, reductions here, changes in various ways; but I do not want at present to yield to the temptation of opening up new fields of taxation. I am going to ask the House and the country to bear patiently for a year or two, perhaps, the condition of affairs, in the hope that the betterment which, we believe, is near at hand, will enable us to bear the burdens without opening up these new fields of taxation to which I refer. I am, therefore, going to ask the House to take the result that we may have to add some little amount to the public debt even yet, rather than introduce new forms of taxation.
It is true that we are adding to the public debt each year, but I note with satisfaction that the amount of the addition is each year diminishing. The figures of our additions to the debt immediately before the war, during the war years and in the years since the armistice, are encouraging. I will now give the round millions. In the meantime it is worth noting that the French Treaty will not be in operation for some weeks. The formalities in closing a treaty generally take time, and we need not be alarmed at any immediate danger in that respect. With regard to the excise duty on wines, as this reduction is intended to offset the provisions of the French Treaty, it will only be brought into operation by proclamation at the same time as the treaty comes into force.
In the observations I have made to-day it will be noticed that I am not touching the Income tax. If there be necessary changes in this respect they will be dealt with later in a separate bill.
/*"'Among the taxes imposed last year was an increase in the duty on cigarettes. Ministers of Finance always look upon tobacco and cigarettes as easy marks-if you ever want a few million dollars just clap an extra duty on tobacco and cigarettes. There was a time when whiskey bore this burden, but additional revenue is no longer possible from this source. I confess I thought last year we might get more money by increasing the duty on cigarettes by $1.50 per thousand. However, the figures seem to show there is a falling off \ in the consumption of cigarettes. My own ' judgment is that there is no falling off in the consumption, the only falling off is in that portion of the commodity which pays duty. Along the boundary line, I am informed, it is a very easy matter to smuggle cigarettes. There are articles which cannot well be smuggled, and there are articles which may be smuggled very easily. Unfortunately, cigarettes come within the latter class. However, our expectations in regard to this tax have not been realized, and we propose now to strike off the extra $1.50 duty and revert to V^the old rate.
There were other disappointments. We thought we might get some money from an excise tax on beetroot sugar, but nothing has come of that. The trade interested has complained very much; no revenue has come to us; and, as I am proposing some readjustment of the sugar duties in other directions, we have concluded to abolish the tax on beetroot sugar.
There were several taxes which caused a good deal of irritation, among others the soft-drink taxes. We propose to change the form of these, and instead of 5c. per gallon and 5 per cent, we propose to strike that business at

its source by imposing a tax cf one cent per pound on carbonic acid gas. We think we will get our money to the same extent and with less trouble.
Customs Tariff Changes	~-
Wre are not making many changes in the details of the Customs tariff. I will mention some, others will be found in the resolutions by those who study them carefully Nearly every item I shall mention is in the direction of reduction. It is a rare thing in this budget to have any proposal to increase taxation, but there is an exception in the item I am about to mention. We are proposing to increase the duty on raisins and dried currants so they will be free from Great Britain and pay 3 cents a pound under both the other tariffs. My hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Robb) recently made a trip to Australia in the hope of coming to a commercial arrangement with the Australian Commonwealth. As we know, wliile he made some progress which gave him some encouragement, he was not able to conclude an agreement. We are advised that in addition to our British preference which we offer to the Australians they are particularly interested in raisins and dried currants, and if we change our tariff so as to offer some inducement to them on these items it will go far to make them content with our scheme and bring about an agreement. In the hope that that may be the case, we are going to provide that the duty on raisins and dried currants shall be increased to 3 cents a pound under the intermediate and under the general tariff, but that they shall be free under the British preference. If Australia makes an agreement, and thus comes under the benefit of the Biitish preference, this will be the rate which will be imposed upon the things that she is most anxious to send us. There is a small duty on raisins and dried currants now.	^

speechtext:
A new induitry ls promised us for the manufacture of artificial silk. It is represented to us that this industry will employ j a large amount of labour and we have everv reason to believe that if we can make en-| couraging terms a great industry will be established. We propose to make a classification in which it will be treated largely | as silk, and we have every reason to hope this will lead to a very important industry ' beipg_gstablished._____________.- 

We proposes to adhere to and extend the British preferential tariff. Our proposal is that on whatever duty may be payable according to the varying rates of the British preferential tariff a discount of 10 per cent shall be allowed. This, of course, does not mean a 10 per cent reduction of the tariff rate. Where the tariff rate is 30 per cent the discount of 10 per cent will reduce it to 27 cents; where the tariff rate is 25 per cent, the discount rate will reduce it to 22i per cent, and so forth. To these reductions we attach two qualifications, the first of which is that they shall not apply in the case of any article where the duty is not above 15 per cent. A duty of 15 per cent will not be regarded as a high one, and it will hardly be expected that we ought to apply these reductions to items which stand at 15 per cent or less. That is one important qualification. There is another one, however, which I am sure the House will receive with satisfaction; we say that this 10 per cent discount shall only apply when the goods are brought direct to the ports of Canada. With Montreal and Quebec in summer, Halifax, St. John, Victoria, Vancouver, and Prince Rupert all the year round, Canada has abundant opportunity to bring her goods into her own ports. We think this is an important step in the direction of the encouragement that many people in our ports have long desired. In this part of our programme we believe we are doing three things which are worthy of commendation. In the first place, there is a comprehensive reduction of duties-and that will be agreeable to those who regard the tariff as a tax. Then, there is an emphasis given to the British preference, which has always found favour among the people of Canada, and then at the end we have this effort to do something for the encouragement of our own ports. We hope the proposal made in this respect will meet with the satisfaction of the House; I am sure it will.
I mentioned that we were having some revision or readjustment of sugar duties. Increases of taxes on commodities are quick to reach the consumer; reductions of taxation on like articles are slower in their operation. The reductions which I have already mentioned will in. due time represent a substantial diminution of the burden of taxation.
Sugar Duties
There is another item on another article of commerce to which I now wish to invite the attention of the House. If there is one , article of almost universal use among our 1 people, it is sugar. Taxation on sugar is a burden on the whole people, and a reduction of the duty on sugar is one of the most direct methods of granting relief. During the war sugar advanced to very high prices. After the war there was for some time a reduction
The Budget-Mr. Fielding

until prices became somewhat normal. Quite recently, however, we Beem to be returning to war-time conditions with respect to the cost of sugar. Just what may be the cause of this advance is perhaps a matter of controversy. In some quarters it is alleged that speculators in the United States have obtained control of the market and that this is the cause of the rapid increase of prices. But one thing that the consumers distinctly know is that they are again called upon to pay very high prices for this very necessary article of household use. In the United States the feeling is so strong that householders in many places are' organizing boycott campaigns against the use of sugar. Nothing of the kind has yet occurred with us, but the consumer is everywhere feeling keenly the burden of the high cost. If, then, we would make Borne very substantia! reduction of taxation, something having a direct bearing on the cost of living, what article is so suitable for the purpose, under present conditions, as the article of sugar? We propose a reduction of 50 cents per 100 pounds on refined sugar and a proportionate reduction on the raw sugar from which the refined article is made. I estimate that in this item we relieve the consumers of sugar of taxation to the extent of $2,500,000.
There is another point I should mention in connection with sugar duties. You know that we have in our tariff what is called the dumping duty, which is designed to apply where illegitimate competition is taking place. There are some lines of trades in which it has not been deemed necessary to apply it; the dumping duty does not apply to refined sugar imported from the United Kingdom. So long as sugar is at a moderate price, that may be all right; the dumping duty would be applied in the case of importations from other countries. But if sugar is going to be at a very high price, as it is now, with the prospect of going higher, then we think a restriction of the dumping duty should apply, and we propose that wherever sugar costs at the point of shipment more than 8 cents per pound, the dumping duty shall hereafter not apply-that is, there will be freedom of purchase irrespective of dumping duty.
Copper Bounty
We have been asked from time to time to do something to encourage industries of various kinds. Where these applications take the form of a request for higher duties, the problem is not an easy one. One of the difficulties of such a situation is
4 p.m. that there are many items in the tariff which cannot stand alone IMr. Fielding.]
for consideration; they are closely related to one another. The article which is the finished product of .one man is practically the raw material of another, perhaps of several others. If you increase duties to assist the first man, you disturb the whole scale and all the others will expect compensatory increases. Industrial aid of this kind naturally meets with widespread objection. There is another form in which it may be possible to assist industry without the disturbing results I have mentioned. The granting of a bounty simplifies the case. Many people, willing to see industry aided, would prefer the bounty rather than protective duties, especially if the bounty be of a temporary character and placed on a sliding scale. One merit of the bounty system is that you know precisely what you are paying and can compare the cost with the results. We have given careful consideration to requests made to us on behalf of the copper interests of Canada. Canada is a copper-producing country. Our far western province, British Columbia, is rich in this respect. Yet the copper industry has made but moderate progress. There is a duty of 1-| cents per pound on copper in the form of ingots. A very large enterprise has been established in British Columbia which is encouraged by this duty. The next stage of the copper business is the production of bars and rods, which become the raw material of other manufactures, such as the making of wire. Copper bars and rods are the raw material of wire manufacturers. To assist them, these bars and rods were some years ago placed on the free list for the use of manufacturers in their own factories. All these bars and rods are thus imported free. Neither of these copper products is produced in Canada for the reason that our producers are unable to compete with large manufacturing enterprises in the United States. We sympathize very warmly with the desire to have a larger development of the copper industry in the Dominion. Since a duty on bars and rods would probably necessitate increased duties on the manufactures of a number of articles made from copper, we are unwilling to grant aid in that form. We have concluded that if the copper industry is to be encouraged as we would desire, it will be better to deal with it directly in the way of a bounty than by higher duties on that which is the raw material for other factories. I said that a bounty will be regarded by many as a better form of aid than any increase of protective duties. But even a bounty would be objected to with much reason if it were not of a temporary character. Much has been heard in times past of the importance of assisting infant in-

The Budget-Mr. Fielding
dustries. Most folk will be kindly disposed towards the industries while they are in their infancy. But experience has shown that the infant grows up, and when he has attained to all the strength of manhood he is still found clinging to protective duties and claiming that he cannot live without them. A new industry which is to have that kind of experience is not a very desirable one for the country. An industry based upon the natural resources of the Dominion which wants a helping hand at the beginning and is prepared later to rely on its own strength and character is worthy of consideration. We propose to afford a measure of help to the copper industry of Canada on the condition that that help shall take the form of a bounty, that the amount of the bounty shall be held within proper limits and that it shall be reduced from year to year until it is extinguished. We propose to allow a bounty for a period of five years, beginning at 1J>
cents per pound and diminishing from year to year until the end of the five-year term. The bounty will apply to copper bars and copper rods manufactured in Canada, from copper produced in Canada, and sold for consumption in Canada, and not to include exports. The privilege now granted to manufacturers to import copper rods and bars for their purposes free of duty will continue. What we desire is that the aid we are giving will enable the Canadian producers to compete as they have not been able to compete before with their American rivals and that they will get a reasonable command of the market. We are placing a limitation of $200,000 per anum upon this bounty. At the beginning the industry will not earn anything like that. As the time rolls on it will probably earn that much, but when it gets to its highest point it cannot get more than $200,000 in any one year.
Bounty on Hemp
There is another industry to which we are going to extend similar aid. We have been working together to encourage the cultivation of hemp, for which article we are assured the soil of parts of our country is particularly adapted. It is believed that with some encouragement a large manufacturing plant can be established in Manitoba, drawing its raw material from the crop to be raised in the immediate vicinity. Here again is a case, where the helping hand may only have to be extended at the beginning. There is a large market in Canada for products manufactured from hemp, and other articles of similar character. If we can economically produce the hemp ourselves and turn it ini a manufactured products in factories within easy
reach of the fields in which it grows, surely that is an industry which may be well worthy of the helping hand. We therefore propose to apply in this case substantially the same rule as in the case of the copper industry. Under the aid we are affording, copper rods and bars should be turned out in Canada at an early date. The development of the hemp business will be slower. To complete the plans of the authorities who are giving attention to the promotion of the movement, to raise the crop and to prepare and manufacture the hemp, will take a considerable time. Ws therefore propose that in this case the five year period shall begin on the first day of July, 1925. By that time binder twine and other products made from Canadian hemp should be ready for the market and the producers will be in a position to claim the bounty. In this case also we propose a bounty beginning at one and one-half cents per pound on the hemp and diminishing from year to year, until at the end of the five years the bounty is extinguished.
In this case, too, we limit our payment to $200,000 per annum. A much less sum would be sufficient at the beginning, but as the enterprise develops its business may be large enough to absorb the full $200,000.
Bounties Granted and Bounties Withdrawn
We are proposing the granting of certain bounties to develop new industries. Let me now draw attention to our desire to put an end to some bounties-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY HON. W S. FIELDING, MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before you leave the Chair, I desire to make a few remarks which I am able to do more easily because my friend was kind enough to let me have information as to some of his figures this morning. Before dealing with the budget, I would like to present my compliments and congratulations to my hon. friend. It is a very nice thing to be able to do that which you like to do and have pleasure in doing. I have great pleasure in congratulating my hon. friend on the presentation of his seventeenth budget. It is hard to realize that this is his seventeenth budget, because he is showing such an evidence of youth all the time. You know, Mr. Speaker, that the supreme evidence of youth is the ability to learn, and I want to congratulate him upon the manner in which he is still learning and taking his lessons to heart. Last year we told him in connection with the cigarette tax what was going to happen, that we had there a tax so high that if anything higher was tried it would kill business and destroy the revenue. My hon. friend said "No, we are going to get an increase of half a million." But there is a drop in the revenue of $1,200,000. But the 1694
hon. minister is not the Bourbon that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Lapointe) is so fend of speaking of. He sees the figures, he learns and he repents. Further than that we told him what would happen in the case of the beet sugar tax. That was a tax that was directly against the farmer and against a primary producing industry, we told him what would happen. Again he has learned, and he has taken the duty off. Besides that, my hon. friend is showing what an apt pupil he is of to-day's conditions. We know he had a great deal of trouble with the French Treaty, and we explained, and explained and explained in this House just exactly my hon. friend's errors in connection with that treaty; -how if he had first had a duty on luxuries which he was dealing with, that would have enabled him to get a proper treaty with France. We are again delighted to get this further evidence of my hon. friend's youthfulness of mind and adaptability, because to-day he turns around, applies what we have been saying, and tells us that the one real excuse for the imposition of a three-cent per pound tax on raisins and dried currants as against a three-quarter-cent per pound tax at the present time is simply because, if that is done, there is some opportunity of making a proper trade treaty with Australia. Again I congratulate my hon. friend; but most of all I desire to congratulate him upon his newfound faith. When I say "new," I say "new" simply because I have reference to what my hon. friend has said time and again from this very seat on the tariff issue. Why, he finds to-day that there is necessity for stability in business. It has taken him a long time to find that out.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT BY HON. W S. FIELDING, MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Some hon. members laugh, but the other day we had a discussion as to what is going on in the United States and the reasons therefor. There is progress there; they have no idea that this manufacturer or that manufacturer, or this kind of business or that, is to be put out of business overnight. They are not drifting; they have some idea where they are going. Yes, they have prosperity in the United States, and my hon. friend says that times have been bad in Canada. But my hon. friend now thinks there is a real necessity for business stability in Canada, and that you cannot have business stability unless you have tariff stability.
My hon. friend has made another wonderful discovery, which I think is the most hopeful

The Budget

Sir Henry Drayton
discovery of them all, namely that the tariff is a low tariff. My hon. friend is absolutely and perfectly right. But I do not like to leave the situation as my hon. friend leaves it. I do not think Canada is in such an awful position as he seems to think. It is true that we are not doing as well as other countries. I do not know that it is incumbent upon the opposition to give apologies and reasons for that. It is true that only last session we were found, by the government that came into power, to be in a better position that any other country was in. But, notwithstanding the fact that we are suffering from a delayed and repressed recovery in this country, it is also true that you cannot keep Canada down, and we are going ahead now. Our trade figures are not bad figures now, although they ought to be better. While our trade figures are not what other countries have had, while we cannot point to the tremendous changes that they can point to in the Mother parliament, while we are piling up deficits as against surpluses reported in the Mother parliament, yet the country itself, the real fundamental business of the country itself, is, at the bottom, sound. We are increasing our exports; we are increasing our activities to some extent, although not as much as I would like to see them increased; but Canada is sound, and Canada will come through, no matter what government is in power.
I want to make just one or two remarks as to the figures submitted by my hon. friend. In the first instance, he very fairly pointed out that the kind of surplus we have to-day is an old story. We had the same thing before. In 1921, we had a surplus of $150,000,000, and still we had a very large increase in our debt. In 1922, we had a surplus of $115,000,000. It is also true, as my hon. friend says, that our whole financial trouble at the present time really has reference to the railway situation. I am going to ask my hon. friend hereafter just to pay a little more attention to that railway situation. I cannot understand how it is that the railways this year cost this country $92,000,000, unless it be that the new management wanted so to swell the vote and the expenses this year that, perforce, an excellent showing must be made next year. Look at the report brought down by the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham). That hon. gentleman made, as we all thought, a good showing this year. In the year 1920, I think we had a deficit of $36,000,000. In the year 1921. we had a deficit of $16,000,000, a reduction of practically $20,000,000. For the year 1922, we had this year a report read on the floor of the House that

there was an operating surplus df $4,000,000 as against a deficit the year before 6f $16,000,000. Yet, in some way or another, the full appropriation asked for, an appropriation which was asked for on the figures of the year before-and though an appropriation is asked for, it is never intended that the money shall be spent unless it is absolutely necessary to spend it-amounts to $92,190,000 which has been drawn on account of railways. I do not know, of course, why it is drawn or anything about it; but without knowing much about it, I suggest to my hon. friend that he should do just this simple little thing-look into the details of the appropriation as made by him last year, check those details and see just how much money has had to be switched from one detail to another in order to make up that amount. I am sure that is something to which my hon. friend may very well give his strictest attention.
Just another word as regards the accounts. My hon. friend points out that we are going behind. So we are. As he told us, the deficit, the addition to the debt before other matters are taken into consideration, will be $61,000,000. Then we have refunds of exchanges, and the net result of it all is, as he tells us, to bring the net addition to the debt down to $49,000,000. The refunds of exchanges amounting to $8,000,000, cannot, of course, be taken into consideration in this year's operations, because they have nothing to do with that at all. That exchange was earned years ago, and the amount Was simply fixed this year. If that were not taken into consideration, we have an addition of $57,492,339 to our debt.
That is the addition to the debt which flows out of the operations of the government this particular year; and my hon. friend I am afraid is sending us off, not with a benediction on this year's work, but practically with an admonition to look to a deficit of $58,000,000 next year, because he tells us that his estimated surplus next year will be $14,100,000 apart from railway obligations. Well, Mr. Speaker, I think that the situation is really a little better than that; I think that probably my hon. friend is taking too gloomy a view of matters, just as I thought he did last year. Last year his estimate for customs was $103,000,000; he has collected over $15,000,000 more, so that he is out in that respect about fifteen per cent. In other words, his spectacles were fifteen per cent too black in that case. Then again, in the case of the income tax, his estimate was $60,000,000; in this direction he was out 812,797,000 or over twenty-one per cent. The thing that is extraordinary to me

Combines
is this, that my hon. friend to-day-that is, assuming that I took down his statement correctly-discounts the collections on income and excess business taxes some 817,797,000. I think that was the figure he gave; he will correct me if I am wrong. Surely my hon. friend is not taking the view that the country is in as bad a position as that estimate indicates. Last year we were told in the address that we were in an excellent position; but we were told in the budget of that year that the year previous had been a very bad one. The exact words of my hon. friend were:
This tax is levied on income of the past year, which was not a good business year. Indeed, I think it was a year of exceptional depression.
And in connection with a year of exceptional depression, the year 1921, he wrote down the collections in respect to income and business profits taxes from 8101,500,000 to $60,000,000, yet, as I say, he collected 872,797,000. This year he is going to make his collections on the income tax and the business profits tax materially lower than he made his estimate for a very bad year. What is the trouble? I admit, of course, that my hon. friends have been in power fourteen or fifteen months;
I admit that business has been harassed and bothered by a hundred and one kinds of pin pricking taxation; I admit that we have experienced uncertainty, and all that sort of thing. But I do not think that the effect of my hon. friend's government is as bad as he thinks it is. The year 1921 he told us was a year of exceptional depression. What does my hon. friend call this year? What kind of language would he apply to it if he is to discount our income and excess business taxes still further? Why, Mr. Speaker, he is making the figures in regard to direct taxation and consumptive taxes much worse even than they were last year. The year before that, when we were responsible, we raised, if I remember rightly, 32 per cent of all the revenue from direct taxation, income and business profits taxes. This year so far-and again I am speaking from recollection, although, I think, correctly-the government has raised only 24 per cent. And we used to be chided and scolded all the time because we were not doing a great deal more in that direction. What does my hon. friend think he has done to business?
I want again to congratulate my hon. friend on becoming an advocate of industry. That is another discovery we have made to-day. He wants to help the artificial silk industry: he wants to help the growing of hemp in Canada and the manufacture. We have not had an opportunity yet of going through the resolutions, and I am not going to say anything about that phase of the budget until 1 have had a chance to study these resolutions. The hon. member I have no doubt is sincere in his conversion in this respect. And all this is to be done in the interest of trade and to ensure that stability which he finds so sadly lacking in Canadian industry to-day. I shall not go any further now, Mr. Speaker, and therefore beg to move the adjournment of the debate.
Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.

On section 27-Contempt of registrar or commissioner.
I thought this section was standing over for a definition of the word "insult" by my hon. friend.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: This will have to be left to whomever the remark is addressed to, to decide. The clause is similar to one which is contained in the Combines and Investigations Act, 1910; it is also similar to a clause in the Industrial Disputes Act. This simply protects a registrar or commissioner in the same manner as a judge from being insulted by persons who may appear before him.

The judge of a court determines what is contempt of court and what is not; he has the authority and the qualification to do so. The registrar is not given any authority here, even if he had the qualification to decide what is an insult. I do not know who drafted this bill, nor do I know who drafted many bills that have been brought down this session, but I can tell the Prime Minister who did not draft it. It was never drafted by the Deputy Minister of Justice.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
As I say, that language is taken from the Combines and Investigations Act of 1910- Section 31 of that act reads as follows:
If, in any proceedings before the board, any person wilfully insults any member of the board, or wilfully interrupts the proceedings, or without good cause refuses to give evidence, or is guilty in any other manner of any wilful contempt in the face of the board, any officer of the board or any constable may take the person offending into custody and remove him from the precincts of the board, to be detained in custody until the conclusion of that day's sitting of the board, and the person so offending shall be liable, upon summary conviction to a penalty not exceeding one hundred dollars.
The registrar or the commissioner stands in the place of the board in this bill. I do not think the section is a very important one, but if it seemed wise to give that protection to the members of the board in a former act,
I think it would be equally wise to give it under this.

I doubt if anybody will ever insult the registrar, indeed, I do not know that many will ever see him unless at a social gathering so I would not worry about the substance of the clause. But it just shows bad draftsmanship; nobody is given power to decide what is an insult.
Where does the bad draftsmanship come in in that clause?
Because the registrar is not given any power to decide whether there is any wilful insult or not.
If a man is given power to hold an investigation, it is not unreasonable that he should have the powers of a judge-
Hear, hear.
-in preserving decorum in his courtroom.
Then why not give it to him?
Is not that what the clause gives him?

No, that is just what I am complaining of, he is not given this power at all. He is not to be a judge, so he is not competent to exeicise the powers of a judge. I call the hon. gentleman's attention to this too: the word "combine" is defined in clause 2, but it is used all through the bill just as if it had never been defined at all.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, no.

A combine is defined as something that works to the detriment of the public, and so on, and subsequently the registrar is commissioned to decide whether some combine works to the detriment of the public. I am curious to know who drafted this bill. Will the Prime Minister tell us?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I might satisfv my hon. friend when I mention to him tha-, the bill as drafted was submitted to the Justice department and gone over by its officers and approved.
That was only as to the competency of this House to pass the measure.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Not at all, it was as to the drafting. Particular reference was made to each section.

Will the Prime Minister not tell us who drafted this bill? The English and general structure of the bill is not reviewed by the Justice department except on special occasions. All I can say about the draftsmanship of this clause is that it is no better than the plan and the whole structure of the bill.

Section agreed to.

By section 487 of the Canada Shipping Act apart from the pilotage districts of Montreal, Quebec, St. John and Halifax, the master or mate of any vessel can apply to the pilotage authority to pass an examination as pilot, and the pilotage authority, after the ordinary examinations and upon the payment of the dues, is compelled to deliver a certificate to that master or mate. The object of the resolution and of the bill is, that instead of making this compulsory on the pilotage authority, to make it discretionary. The pilotage authority, instead of "shall deliver the certificate", "may deliver the certificate" after it has approved the request. The necessity for this has been shown to the department in a special case this season in the pilotage district of Mirami-chi. At this place the channel is narrow, and any accident that takes place there would block the traffic altogether. It is not a very important district, and the pilot could not make a living if the most important ships that go there were relieved from the obligation of taking those pilots on those ships. It is very important to the port that pilots should be retained there to bring foreign ships in. The only purpose of the resolution and of the bill which will be introduced based upon it is, in special cases, to empower the pilotage authority to refuse the examination of a master and mate and to place the small pilotage districts on the same level as Quebec,

Montreal, St. John and Halifax in this regard.
Who is the pilotage authority?

The Governor in Council under a section of the Shipping Act can at any time nominate the Minister of Marine and Fisheries as pilotage authority for any port. For the port of Miramichi, for instance, the minister is the authority.

speakeroldname: Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Argenteuil, Acting Minister of Immigration):
speechtext:
When the
bill was last under consideration exception was taken to the amendment to the Immigration Act which is proposed in section 3 of this bill. This section proposes to repeal section 41 of the act and replace it by the old section which was embodied in the act up to the time that the present section was adopted. That old section, which it is now proposed to reenact, provides:
Whenever any person other than a Canadian citizen advocates in Canada the overthrow by force or violence of the government of Great Britain or Canada, or other British dominion, etc.
Objection was taken to the words "any person other than a Canadian citizen" on the ground that they implied a reflection on British subjects who were not Canadians. I propose therefore to strike out the words after the word "any" and substitute in their stead the word "alien," so that the section will now read:
Whenever any alien advocates, etc.
Why not say "any person" instead of "any alien"? There is no reason why a Canadian citizen should not be amenable to the law in this respect.

Immigration Act

The minister has failed to protect himself. An alien is forbidden to advocate the assassination of any official of the government, but apparently he may advocate the assassination of any member of the government.
Which is sometimes justifiable.

speechtext: I am simply adopting the old wording; I have not changed the language of the old section at all. Exception was taken to the fact that, by implication, permission was given the department to deport a British subject, and the amendment I now propose is intended to meet that difficulty.

I am not objecting to the amendment, but I would strike out the words "any official of the government of Great Britain or Canada or other British dominion," etc., and simply say "assassination." I do not know why officials of the government should be particularly sacrosanct.
Particularly if appointed by the Civil Service Commission.
Perhaps it is the immigration agent the minister wants to protect.

Listening to the budget
this afternoon, Mr. Chairman, I thought this provision was going to be dropped, that the withdrawal of the duty on hemp was for the purpose of getting the proper kind of rope for hanging these people instead of sending them out of the country. What'is the purpose of the government?
If the section can be improved why not improve it?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: For ten years we have got along all right with this wording, and it is well to be careful not to change the wording of any particular clause without considering its effect upon other parts of the bill. Yes. Why should it be
any more a deportable offence to advocate the assissination of an official of the government than the assassination of anybody else?

We are also providing
against the assassination of Lenine and Trotsky, because this section applies to all foreign governments.

I submit with a good
deal of confidence that assassination is undesirable under all circumstances, and in regard to all persons, and if it is advisable to retain this clause, I do not see why the words "of any official of the government of Great Britain or Canada, or other British dominion, colony, possession, or dependency, or of any foreign government" should not all be stricken out.
That is what I mean.
Any person who advocates assassination is ipso facto undesirable and should be deported.

Strike out the

Yes.

Assassination applies only
to the murdering of those high in authority, not to ordinary individuals.
Make it apply to ordinary individuals. I want the protection to apply to ourselves.
Should not the word "assassination" be supplemented by another word?

"Assassination"
is a good word. Do you like "murder" better?
I would suggest "assassination or murder."
What is the difference?
There is a legal difference.

Perhaps the section would be clear in this form:
Whenever any person other than a Canadian citizen advocates in Canada the overthrow by force or violence of the goverment of Great Britain or Canada, or other British dominion, colony, possession, or dependency, or the overthrow by force or violence of constituted law and authority, or by assassination, or shall, by word or act, and so on.
The whole idea is to look after assassination which tends to overthrow government.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. H. KING (Minister of Public Works) :
speechtext: The first item 81,500,000, is a vote to continue the construction of a dry-dock at Victoria. Ihe amount of this contract was $4,217,400. In 1921-22 $1,164,872 was expended. Of the apropriation for 1922-23, on the 31st March, $547,700 had been expended.
How near completion is that dry-dock?

The contract expires in January 1924. There have been certain delays and probably an extension will be required. Although the contract should be completed in 1924, I would not think the dry-dock would be ready for operation before 1925.
The government is responsible for the delay. Did the government not hold up the work for quite a while?

There was some
delay last year by the failure to vote supply in the Main Estimates.

The minister sees his error, I hope, and is duly repentant. Has the minister a report that he can lay on the Table, that the government received us to the necessity of this dock, the probable utility of it?

This is not a new project; it has been under consideration for many years. Negotiations were carried on years ago and a site purchased for the construction of this dry-dock. All that went by the board; but in 1919-20, my right hon. friend and his government entered into a contract to construct this dry-dock. There was some hesitation on the part of this government [DOT] as to the advisability at the time, with conditions as they were lollowing the war, of entering into the construction of two dry-docks on the Pacific coast within a few miles of one another. This government, on coming into office, found that an expenditure of $1,000,000 had been made at Victoria, and although there was a doubt as to the advisability of continuing the construction of these two dry-docks, one at Esquimalt and one at Vanvouver, it was considered advisable, after careful investigation had been made, to continue construction of the dry- dock at Victoria. In the Supplementary Estimates of last year, an appropriation of $1,000,000 was passed for continuation of construction, and the work has been proceeding since that time.

The minister stated that this matter was deferred for investigation. What was brought to the minister's attention



Supply-Public Works
during the investigation that contributed to the decision of the government to go on with the work?

I do not think there should be any doubt in my right hon. friend's mind as to the attitude of the government on taking office. The declaration was made by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) when he was contending in the countryside for election and the election of his party, that contracts which had been entered into would be investigated. We found on the Pacific coast that two contracts for dry-dock purposes had been entered into, and these with other contracts were held up. As regards the work at Victoria, as I have already explained to the committee, there had been an expenditure of $1,000,000, and after a thorough investigation and going into the requirements of shipping on the Pacific coast, we concluded we would be well advised to continue construction of that dock.

The minister got to the point at the last minute, but he was not very explicit. The point that I asked him was not as to any historical account. I know that pretty well myself. I asked him what were the results of the investigation that prevailed with the government and decided it to go ahead. He mentions that after investigating the necessities of shipping on the Pacific coast, the government decided to continue the construction. Does he mean by that the government was convinced that the necessities of shipping really required that dry-dock?

After the investigation which the government made, and taking into account the fact that there had been a very large expenditure on the dock and also the increased shipping and development on the Pacific coast, the government was convinced as to the advisability of continuing construction of that dock.

Supposing there had
been nothing at all spent on it, would the government then have seen fit to go on with the work? Did the necessities of shipping so impress the government that it would have gone on with the work even had we not commenced it?
The government in that case would have been in an independent position to make its own investigation and to define its own policy.

The government made an investigation and the minister has the result. Will the minister say to-day that the

late government went on too soon with the construction of the dry-dock?
I would say that that government went on too late. That dry-dock should have been constructed in 19121913. If it had been constructed then, it would have served a useful purpose.
Undoubtedly it would. Then will the minister say that we did not commence it too soon in 1919?

It would have
been very useful during the war period.
Does the minister think we commenced too soon in 1919?

I think it would have been much better to have commenced at an earlier date, as we would then have had the use of the dock during a time when it would have been of great service, not only to British Columbia, but to the Empire generally.

That is not my point, and I do not know why the minister does not answer my question. Perhaps it would have been better if we had known when the war was going to break out. We, however, did not commence the dock in 1912. If we had followed the advice of my hon. friend's friends, there would have been a number of things that we would not have commenced. As, however, we did not commence the dry-dock before the war, or during the war, does the minister say that we were too early in commencing it in 1919? I know this is a poser.

So far as I am concerned there is no poser. My right hon. friend has no reason to worry about my position as regards the dry-dock. My party had, in 1911, a contract for the construction of a dry-dock on the Pacific coast. When we came into power in 1921, we took conditions as we found them, and we are carrying on, I believe, to the satisfaction of the people on the Pacific coast in the matter of dry-dock policy.
That is not what I asked.

I am answering the question and my right hon. friend can interpret my answer. I think it is a fair answer, and so far as I am concerned there was no poser in his question. We are proceeding with the construction of this dry-dock.

The minister is simply dodging the question. I am going to keep

Supply-Public Works
on a little longer, perhaps some time longer.
I am asking the minister: Keeping in mind that we did not commence during the war or before the war, did we commence, under all the circumstances, too early in 1919 at the time we did commence? He can answer that by saying yes or no.
I will give my right hon. friend the same answer that I gave before, that he commenced construction of the dry-dock too late.

How then does the minister justify his support of his leader who denounced us for commencing it too soon? Is that the poser for the hon. gentleman? I do not hear any answer to that. I presume I may assume that this is just another instance of the whole humbug that was perpetrated throughout the entire year. The minister, I presume, by his silence will acquiesce in that description.

We do not need to acquiesce at all. My right hon. friend would like to develop a situation at this time, but the situation is not there for him to develop. If he thinks he can get any glory out of his policy in the matter of dry-docks, he is privileged to take all the glory he can get. As regards ourselves, we are carrying on. I think, in the interests of the country.

I was not seeking glory at all; I was seeking a frank statement from the minister. He declines to answer whether we commenced too soon in 1919 or not. He dodges the question by saying that we should have commenced in 1912. I asked him then: Assuming that we had not commenced in 1912, had not gone on during the war, under all the circumstances did we commence too soon in 1919? He declines to answer.
That is a matter of opinion entirely. My right hon. friend can have his own opinion.
I know my opinion exactly and I will say it. I will say that we did not commence too soon. Will the minister have the courage to say yes or no?

dimensions of the dock are such as to afford sufficient accommodation, I understand, for the largest ships afloat.

However, it was a fad of the hon. minister's predecessor, and no doubt the dock will be useful, but we will never get the full benefit of that expenditure until wharves are put in the basin to connect with the Canadian National Railways, which will mean considerable further expenditure. I am not attacking the minister. He has been down to St. John and I will give him credit for having shown all the interest that could be reasonably expected of a minister. I	think	he is sympathetic.
But I would like to carry the project a little beyond the point of sympathy. The completion of the breakwater is only a matter of good business; indeed, it is vital, for otherwise it will simply be a matter of carrying in a useless condition these other valuable works that have cost a lot of money and on which the country is bearing the interest charge. I would urge as strongly as I can that at least a beginning be made this year. The community of St. John, as the minister knowo and as a good many hon. members know, spent quite largely of its own means to make a winter port out' of the harbour. They have been helped by governments regardless of the political faith of those governments, and more will have to be done. After all, St. John and Halifax are to be the great winter outlets of this country on the Atlantic coast. The community has sent delegation after delegation to government after government here, but one thing after another has turned up. This Courtenay bay project has interfered; the war has interfered; and the difficulty of finance has interfered, and still we find in the winter seasons more vessels-perhaps the condition was not so bad last winder as it had been on previous occasions-lying out in the stream, waiting for berths, than there ought to be. I say it does not make good business in the port- and all the time there are two splendil docks which these vessels cannot utilize because a gap about a quarter of a mile long is not closed between this breakwater and the island. I would like to lend to the minister some of the vehemence that I and the community in general feel like expressing on this subject, so that he might use it in council

Supply-Public Works
with a view to effecting these purposes the consummation of which the whole community so strongly desires.
What would be the estimated cost for the completion of the breakwater?
The last tender we received on that work, I am informed, was $750,000.
When was that tender? Mr. KING (Kootenay): Eight or ten years ago, I believe.
It would be more expensive now. That is the Negro Point breakwater, intended to extend to Partridge island?
Yes.
What amount has been spent on that in the last four or five years.'
This is an extension of work done, I believe, a great manj years ago. I have not before me the figures as to the cost of the original work.
Has no money been spent on it in the last four years?
Only for maintenance and repairs.
Is the work in good shape now as far as it has gone? Is it serving as a breakwater yet, to the extent to which it has been built?
The work was constructed twenty or thirty years ago. I am advised that it is in good condition.

I would join in the appeal of the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Baxter). I visited the district, and it really appears to me that the millions that we have put there are not going to be available for service until that breakwater is completed. The breakwater is the protection of the investment, and I hope it at least will be carried on concurrently with the completion of the other work.
Do I understand that no estimate has been made since the estimate of ten years ago?

No new tenders have been called for since that time. The department has made frequent investigations and estimates, but I do not know that they are below that amount, which was the lowest tender received. Some tenders were as high as a million dollars and more.
I thought it was customary for the department to make some estimate of its own.
There is no item bearing on that, and I have not the information here.

If that is the case, one cannot hope that the matter is being very actively looked into at the present time. I would remind the minister that several years ago there was a natural breakwater there which was removed for the purpose of the extension of the harbour facilities. The Negro Point breakwater has been only partly 9 p.m. completed, so that there has been no entire replacement of the natural breakwater that formerly existed. I am sure the minister will agree as to the reasonableness of the suggestion that the harbour should be put in as good a position as it was in years ago. We are voting $860,000 for the completion of the Courtenay bay works, but we are not providing for the completion of the breakwater which is the protection not only for these works but for the wharves and piers on the other side of the harbour I would urge upon the minister, therefore, the importance of proceeding with this work, not only for the protection of the existing government works, but also to put the harbour in as good a condition as existed previous to the taking away of the natural breakwater.

I assure my hon. friend that we are not unmindful of the matter as it has been pressed by him. It is a question of finance and the ability to do work of this character at the present time. The matter is receiving serious consideration.

I do not want to torture the hon. minister, but earlier in the session he told me that the department was making some further investigation and that he was expecting a further report. Of course I do not know that it would be judicious to have the figures given out if a report has been made, because that might affect any future call for tenders. But if the minister has a further report, I would like to ask whether it shows any serious increase in the cost of doing the work. The condition at the port of St. John probably is of very little interest to a large part of the Dominion, and yet it ought to be of very great interest to those who do not believe that their own locality is the whole of Canada. That condition compels me to say something as to the work that has been done, and the work that is, in a sense, being wasted for want of something more

Supply-Public Works
being done. For a distance of about a quarter of a mile from the main channel of St. John harbour in towards the shore, and for a distance, I would think, of nearly half a mile along the length of the channel, mud and boulders which used to be visible at low tide have been dredged at thirty-two feet below water level. That work cost, if my memory is correct, about 90 cents a cubic yard of material removed. The soil that was removed was carried out beyond this breakwater that we are speaking of. Every tide, and there are two of them a day, brings some of that material back into the big ditch that it cost millions of dollars to make, which was excavated in order to establish wharves for ocean steamers. Two large piers were constructed. Three more, I think, could be constructed and if they were built we would have space for at least a dozen large vessels. We probably do not need all that space at the present moment; but following a course that has been pursued for many years-I am not laying this at the door of the minister alone-the country will be faced sonle time with the necessity of redredging this large area. If we bad that breakwater completed it would save the cost, to some extent, of redredging that area in the future; and I am trying to get the attention of the committee so that the minister may have reasonable support if he comes here at a later stage and says that it is good business to close that gap now, even though we cannot afford to build any more extensive wharves within the area which it protects. I am only appealing in the name of common sense and plain, decent, business economy. I believe the minister is sympathetic. I believe he is convinced of the utility of this work, but I think he fears, because of financial conditions, to put a project-even of the magnitude of perhaps a quarter of a million dollars for a beginning- before the House. I want to encourage him to do so, but I would like to evoke enough real attention and study to this problem, so that members should feel that it was no mere waste of money for the sake of pleasing a locality, but that it was a vital step in " enabling Canada as a whole to handle her traffic within her own ports and borders instead of letting it pass through the ports of a foreign country.
Before the item passes I would like to ask the minister if he expects any extra ports will be needed in eastern Canada in view of the clause contained in the budget speech this afternoon.

Pardon me a moment. I do not know whether the hon. member's re-

mark was intended to be facetious,, or whether it was intended for a sneer but I am going to say that what was announced this afternoon in the budget speech was in my opinion a bigger thing than ordinary politics. It was a realization of the policy of Canada for Canadians, a thing that people with whom I have been associated have been talking of, dreaming of, and hoping for. I am glad to see that at last it is made part of the national policy of Canada, and I am prepared to back up a proposition of that kind no matter by whom, or how, or when it is introduced.
It was the minister's opinion I asked for, Mr. Chairman.
Well, you got mine.

We on this side entertain great hjpes that the tonnage and shipments coming in and going out of Canada will in the course of a few years, under the rule and regime of the Liberal party, be greatly increased not only in the ports on the Atlantic but in those on the Pacific as well.

Before we leave this item, would the minister tell us what progress he has made in relation to the emergency which has arisen in Portage la Prairie? I want to draw attention to one error that the minister made in the previous discussion. He sought to chide me for having neglected to provide, while I was in office and in response, to appeals, for the correction of the error of 1908, in order that water might flow around the bend and thus take care of the sewage. I had no recollection of any appeal whatever, or of the question ever arising. Since then I have obtained from the Department of Public Works a copy of all the correspondence, and I find that my recollection is quite correct. That matter never arose at all. What was appealed for at that time was the dyking of the banks, in order that floods might be prevented. That was under consideration, and reports of engineers were made looking to the curing of the situation arising therefrom, but the matter in issue between my hon. friend and me was a wholly different matter. No appeal was made by the municipality and no appeal was made individually. I draw that fact to the attention of the minister, so that he will not fall into that error in the future, and that he will be more careful in a controversy to adhere to the issue and not to obscure it by something which has nothing to do with it. What progress has been made? He will recall that he stated to the House that it was the intention of the government to provide for
an extension of the sewerage system down to the present flow of the river, providing only that such was constructed at reasonable cost. That was the definite undertaking of the minister? His estimate then of what that would cost was $45,000 which he intended to contribute, but he made the statement very clearly twice, in answer to me, that the government's intention was to provide the extension at whatever cost it might entail; that is the money that would be required to complete it, if it were reasonably conducted. I understand that since he has made an offer wholly different from that. I do not know just what has taken place of recent date, but I hope to get a favourable report from the minister of this subject, and the time is now very close at hand when it will become a matter of increasing seriousness.

In reply to my right hon. friend, I wish to state that there is. no misunderstanding. It is probably not worth while reviewing it, but in 1917 and 1918 the engineering department did request of the government that certain works should be done on the channel that, had been dug in order to prevent what has occurred. My hon. friend suggests that this is not in the correspondence. Well he probably has had more time than I have had. I understand he has had the correspondence, but the reports I had from the engineering department indicated that that was the condition at that time. In regard to the advance that was made since then, I do not think we have much to report to the House. In the previous discussion I suggested to the House that we had an estimate of $45,000. Since that time it has been revised by the engineering department, and we are advised that it can be done for $35,000, and the city of Portage la Prairie has been so advised. Within the last few days there have been tremendous floods in that area, and we are awaiting reports from them. I think the matter will be up for discussion later, when the Supplementary Estimates are before the House.

I have read the correspondence very closely. The minister was complaining that there was no response on the part of the late government. There was no appeal to the late government and no request by anybody. What was requested was a different matter. I know the minister will recall it, if he will wait until I have made my assertion. I am aware that the minister of the time obtained a report from the engineers, in response to an appeal for dyking the river, not to any appeal with respect to the sewerage at all. The matter never came up, and
Supply-Public Works

would not come up till there was some need of it. In response to that appeal the engineer recommended that certain things be done with a view to meeting the situation, and, incidentally, in the course of that report stated that it would have the other effect as well. The weir would provide for the water flowing round the bend. That was a wholly different matter. How could he suggest that the failure to provide the weir was at the door of the late government, when the jnatter was never called to their attention? Nobody drew it to their attention. The correspondence clearly disposes of that. So much for that subject. The minister had no warrant to inject into the controversy anything in the way of a remonstrance against, the administration in relation to the bend in the river and the sewerage. Now the minister revises his estimates, but does he not see that that does not affect the issue at all, because the minister's undertaking in the House was, provided of course the city were satisfied to accept it, that the government was prepared to provide as much money as was reasonably necessary to continue that sewerage system down to where the water actually flows? Is the minister still ready to abide by that?

I have had the opportunity of reading a letter addressed by my right hon. friend to the mayor of Portage la Prairie following the discussion recently on this item, and I have no doubt a similar letter will be written to-morrow to the mayor of Portage la Prairie, advising the mayor as to how he held the minister up, and how he made the minister say this and that. There is no doubt in regard to the position of the government. My hon. friend says there is no responsibility on his part, and that no representations were made. Who are the agents of the government? The Public Works engineer in that district, who did make reports, advised that a weir be put in in order that the water might go round the bend and prevent what has happened. Now I can quite understand that my right hon. friend, although a member of the government, might never have heard of that before. It is quite easy to understand that, but I claim that the agents of the government did foresee the danger at that point and recommended to the government that certain works should be undertaken.

There was no mention of the danger whatever-not the least. The report simply stated that this would meet the request for dyking the river, and at the same time would provide a weir for turning the water
lMr. Meighen. J
round. No government in the world would propose to provide against a contingency that was never called to its attention. The minister tries to intimate to the House that I wrote an unfair letter to the mayor at Portage la Prairie. I would ask him to read that letter.

I do not have it
here.

I do not think the minister should have so intimated. I merely stated the facts to the mayor, and I transmitted Hansard in order that the city would know where it stood. That was my plain duty to the council of Portage la Prairie. I recited what had taken place in no boastful tone at all. I think it is the duty of one who interests himself in this matter-and I take some interest in it, and I have some interest in it from many standpoints-to report what does result. That alone was done. I think it is the duty of the minister to state the position of the department fairly. I ask him, is he still ready to do that? I do not know that it will be of any value, but it may be. I know the city council feels that it should not be saddled with the cost of maintenance of that extra sewerage outlet, which I think is about a mile and a half, some considerable distance at all events. They feel that the government is fully responsible and should bear that cost. Is the minister prepared to abide by what I understood to be his undertaking before, which I never thought he would have varied, save by reason of the intimation that since has been given to the city council. Has the minister's undertaking been in any way varied?

I am sorry I was not in at the opening of this discussion, but evidently the hon. member for Grenville (Mr. Meighen) is discussing matters pertaining to Portage la Prairie. About two weeks ago, while I was out of the House temporarily, word was sent to me that he was also discussing Portage la Prairie. He was finished when I got in; but on reading Hansard I noticed that he said he should apologize. I would like to accept the apology, but I am afraid he is unrepentant. As hon. members no doubt are aware, I am fully conversant with matters pertaining to Portage la Prairie. I have worked in connection with this matter; I have done all I possibly could, and I may say that the government have met our request in a favourable mood. I think they have offered to do what I believe is the square thing. They have offered to take care of the sewage system in Portage la Prairie and replace it, put it back where they found

Supply-Public Works
it. I do not think you could ask the government to do anything further than that, and I do not believe the people of Canada, much as I respect my constituents and all that, could be expected to take care of the sewage system of Portage la Prairie forever.
If the government will assume responsibility for the situation which has developed there, if they will go so far as to put the situation back as they found it, they cannot be expected to go further than that, and the citizens of Portage la Prairie would consider that they were only doing their duty in that regard. The Minister of Public Works speaks of a letter that the hon. member for Grenville sent to the Portage la Prairie Graphic.
I am responsible for handing that paper to the minister, and to show that the hon. member for Grenville is a third-rate politician. I would be glad if the minister would read that letter to the committee to-night.

I wish to pursue the subject just a little further. If the minister will state that the undertaking is as stated by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie, I am quite content. That will suit me exactly. If the government is really in the position that it is prepared to put the city as it was, from which place it was dislodged by the action of the former government, of course a Liberal government, that is quite satisfactory to me, and I am prepared to accept that wholly.

This matter seems to be of very considerable interest to my right hon. friend, and it has been pursued to some extent. I am going to take occasion just now to make a reference to the hon. member who represents Portage la Prairie. He has given us valuable assistance. Last summer, during the harvest season, when he was busily engaged in his home work, he left the fields, took the train hurriedly, made a trip to Ottawa and laid this whole matter before the government or the Department of Public Works. He also brought up the question of certain river bank protection. We have had investigations made since then, and w'e have carefully followed the matter. Why my right hon. friend should want to pursue this matter to-night when the item is not under discussion, when a little later on, as he knows, Supplementary Estimates will be up, and this subject will be up for discussion, and to have me reaffirm the statement I made some two or three weeks ago, I cannot understand, except that I am advised that the mayor representing the city council of Portage la Prairie is now on his way to Ottawa, in order that he may further pursue this subject. The department's mind is made up; it
was freely expressed to my right hon. friend and to members of the committee not long ago. We have not changed our minds, and my right hon. friend, who has recently perused the files, knows from his perusal that there is a letter setting forth to the mayor of Portage la Prairie the undertaking which the government are prepared to make in that matter. Why we should be pressed to reiterate a statement to-night, I cannot for the life of me see. It may be the desire of the right hon. gentleman to make representations at this time, before the mayor who is now on his way here at the expense of the citizens of Portage la Prairie has an opportunity of making his representations.

I knew the matter was
discussed as to the mayor coming down. I did not know that it had been decided that he should come.' I was anxious for the reaffirmation, for Only one reason as I explained, because the letter of the minister was not strictly in accord with the undertaking as I understood it. He now says that the government has not changed its mind. That is satisfactory to me, and I am glad to have an intimation that the subject is to be taken care of in the Supplementary Estimates.

If I am in order I should
like to say another word.
