Supply-Public Works
What was spent last year?
The total vote was expended.
What is the difference between the government telegraph lines and the telegraph lines operated in connection with the railways?

The telegraph and telephone service of the- government has been largely a pioneer service. These lines have been built to remote places that have not been attractive enough for private capital. The lines have served a very useful purpose. There is a marked difference between our telegraph lines and those of the railways. As I have said, we reach remote places whereas the railway telegraph lines serve those territories tributary to the railways. We are now trying to unload certain of this work in territories served by the railways which have recently been acquired, and there has been co-operation between the railways and the Dominion telegraph service.
What department, undertakes the collection of the revenue from these lines?
The work is done by our department.

I see that the expenditure on the whole of this item No. 360 is somewhat less than it was last year. Would he tell the committee how much revenue came from the whole of these different lines of telephone?

I am sorry I have not that information. In this detailed statement of expend'tures the revenue collected apparently is not taken into account. I shall be pleased to give my hon. friend that information at an early date.
Could the minister give a rough estimate?
I would hesitate to do so, but I can inform my hon. friend that the service is being run at a loss.

I took it for granted. Of course, I know a great deal of this work is being done for the benefit of sections of the country which are non-revenue producing to a great extent, but it would be interesting to know in a general way if we are losing 50 per cent, 25 per cent, or what percentage on such an item.
In the printed annual report of the Public Works department the required particulars will be found.
Between what points are these lines run in Saskatchewan that entail this expenditure?

In Saskatchewan, Qu'Appelle-Onion Lake section, 63 miles; Battleford-Isle La Grosse section, 298 miles; Moose Jaw-Willow Bunch section, 212 miles, making a total ot 573 miles. The department is arranging to abandon certain lines in that area. There will be a considerable expenditure incurred in taking down the pole lines and salvaging the material, but eventually a saving of $10,000 or $12,000 a year will be effected.
Are these lines built entirely at the expense of the Dominion, or is there any contribution towards their cost by the provinces and the municipalities?

There will be some minor extensions. These will appear in the supplementary votes probably. They usually come up from year to year.

Yes.

The statutory increases account for $13,100. There are 38 transfers from other appropriations, seven from Works salaries, sixteen from Engineering salaries, fourteen contingencies and one Ottawa building repair appropriation, making a total of $63,300. There has been a decrease due to six resignations, eight retirements, two deaths, and four transfers, three from civil government and one to civil government. The total decrease amounts to $20,115. There is a net increase of $61,265. As a matter of fact the pay-roll of the department is less this year than last.
That is including temporary and permanent employees?
Yes.

I do not know what the policy in the past was, but I notice this session the same reply has been given in regard

to various other departments-that the increase in salaries is because a number of temporary employees have been made permanent. Is that a new policy, or has the government decided upon this procedure for all the departments?

It had been the practice in the government service for a man who got a position to be appointed temporarily, on probation, and as time passed he either got a position in the permanent service or did not. In the blanketing-in lists recently adopted in my department there were men who had held important positions in the service for quite long periods of time. One was an engineer who had been in the service some twenty years. In the case of persons holding positions of a permanent character, doing work which is of value in the service, there has been a disposition to make them permanent. This is carrying out a policy adopted by the late government following the reclassification and rearrangement of the service It makes the estimate before us look larger, but where this item has been increased others have been reduced. The employees concerned are merely transferred from one pay roll to another.

I entirely agree that when a man has been for some years in a temporary position he might well be put on the permanent list. But has there been any systematic policy under which a man is transferred to the permanent staff after having been on the temporary list a certain length of time?
No definite policy.
Was there no method by which a man would be automatically transferred to the permanent staff after having been on the temporary list, say, two or three or four years?

I understand that those who were brought in by order in council were considered permanent employees; others remained on the temporary list. But since 1919, after the reclassification, there has been a disposition to place on a permanent basis persons who have been in the service many year's and are performing important duties.

I think that is a proper policy. The minister mentions the case of an engineer who had been twenty years on the temporary staff. It seems a ridiculous thing that a man like that, apparently a capable employee, should work so long and only at the end of the twentieth year be placed on the permanent list. I suggest that it would be

Supply-Public Works
worth the minister's consideration and the time of some of his colleagues to endeavour to work out some scheme whereby a person listed as temporary who had given efficient service and performed necessary duties for a given length of time should be transferred to the permanent staff.

As appointments
are made now, they are given by the Commission either permanent or temporary standing; they enter the service on that definite basis. At present, therefore, there is not so much difficulty on that score.
Can the minister say how many temporary employees there still are-in other words, how many have not been transferred to the permanent staff?

I have not that list here, but it has been worked out in the department. There is a very large number of employees who are not on the permanent list-caretakers, elevator attendants, firemen, engineers, and so on. Many of them work at prevailing rates. Under this vote we show thirty-eight employees as having been brought in and classed as permanent.

Thirty-eight temporary
employees?

Clerical and technical temporary employees who
10 p.m. have been in the department for some years and whose services are
necessary.
What are the occasions which necessitate appointments to temporary positions in the department?

Pressure of work. Years ago appointments were made to important positions and permanent standing might not be given for a considerable length of time. When extra work makes temporary appointments necessary, the commission now issues a certificate designating the appointment as temporary.

These employees, I
assume, would know that their appointment was temporary and that their services might be dispensed with at any time?
Yes.
How does the personnel compare in number with that of the previous year?
There is a decrease of twenty from last year.

Item agreed to.
National Monument on Connaught place, $10,000.

When we were in committee before, this item was held up at the request of one or two members, who had some hesitancy about voting an expenditure of 810,000 in connection with the building of a national monument on Connaught place. I am rather sorry the Prime Minister is not in his seat because he would express more felicitously the desire of the government in this matter than I can. It has been felt by the government that we should erect something in the nature of a national monument in the capital city of Canada to commemorate the deeds of our men overseas, a monument of a national character such as would express the sentiment of the nation in that regard. As I say some objection was taken when the vote was brought forward but I do not think it is at all unreasonable-in view of the fact that we have undertaken the expenditure of a very large sum of money in France to erect fitting memorials to the heroism and endurance of our soldiers in the Great War-that we should ask for a small expenditure at this time in order that plans and designs might be prepared for the erection of a permanent memorial in Ottawa to indicate to the world Canada's opinion of the gallant part Canadians played in that struggle. The opinion of competent authorities will be sought in choosing a suitable design, and we are asking for the present amount in order that the work may be started and carried to a successful completion.
Does the present amount cover the cost of preparing plans?
It is just a preliminary amount.
I notice on the central pillar at the entrance to these buildings an inscription denoting that it has been erected in recognition, among other things, of the valour of our men who went overseas?
Yes.
It is now proposed to have a second memorial? In what respect does the present memorial fall short of its purpose?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Perhaps I
might say a word as to what the government had in mind in making this proposal. In every country in the world the spirit of the nation has found some expression in regard to great events in the form of permanent monuments if the occasions have been sufficiently worthy of such recognition from the national point of view. The government felt that a
Supply-Public Works

monument should be erected in the capital of Canada expressive of the feelings of the Canadian people as a whole to the memory of those who had participated in the Great War and had lost their lives in the service of humanity. The thought was that the most appropriate centre in the capital should be chosen for such a monument. I may say, without suggesting any finality in the matter, the idea was that something in the nature of a great column erected in the triangle just opposite the post office, which is the very centre of the city of Ottawa, would be the most suitable form of monument and locality. My hon. friend (Mr. MacLaren) has referred to the column in the parliament buildings; I think he has reference to the central pillar in the main entrance. That column has an inscription on it commemorative of the services of our men in the Great War. I do not think it is intended as a national monument in any sense of the word. The same column contains a commemorative reference to confederation. Indeed, I think the pillar is more or less symbolical of our relations with the British Empire as a whole; the column arising out of a symbolical sea being representative of the British Isles and the dominions whereas the columns on each side are symbolical of the various provinces of the Dominion. I believe the architect's whole plan is more or less symbolical of these ideas. But the monument to be erected to commemorate the deeds and services of those who participated in the Great War is intended to be a national monument in the national capital. There are in many Canadian cities monuments which those cities themselves have erected; but there is, as yet, no monument of a national character in the capital of the Dominion. The government has received representations from different quarters that such a monument was rather expected on the part of the Canadian people. Even if such representations had not been received the government would have felt that having regard to the events of the past, the part which Canada took in the war, and the valour of her sons, something of the kind commemorative of their heroism, sacrifice and service, should be erected in the capital of our country.
W'hat is the estimate of the total cost?
That will largely depend on the design that is accepted.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think the custom, in most cases of this kind, is to ad-
vertise the purposes in view and call for designs from architects and sculptors, leaving to a committee the choice of a suitable design and to fix the maximum of expenditure.
I should think the government would have in mind some maximum of expenditure for a monument of this kind.

I would say offhand $50,000 or $75,000 but I am speaking without any knowledge of the nature of the design and what may be recommended. We must, if we decide to erect a monument, make a start. Designs having been received, it will be the duty of those who have to make the choice to make a suitable selection. Then we can come to parliament and ask for a sufficient vote to carry the proposition out.

It seems to me that at this time a protest ought to be made against the government going on with a work of this character and that on several grounds. First of all we should not be asked to make a preliminary grant without having some very definite idea as to the actual expenditure involved. If this $10,000 is spent on plans we shall probably have the government coming next year w-ith a very elaborate scheme and one of the pleas for a larger expenditure will be that this vote has been spent and it ought not to be spent in vain. At this time when we are trying to save money, and restricting departmental expenditures which could render necessary services and desirable to the people, I think we might very well economize on such a project as this. There are people all over this country who are struggling to meet the enormous burdens of debt that we are now carrying. We are adding, this year, we were told only this afternoon, $50,000,000 more of debt. I speak for at least one section of the people when I say that, however desirable it may be to add works of art to the capital, we ought not at this particular time, with the people burdened with debt as they are, to incur any more expense than is absolutely essential. Further than that, there are a great many of those who went overseas who are not fully provided for at the present time. This government cannot see its way to provide anything for the unemployed, and there are thousands of men who spent several years overseas who are to-day suffering and vrhose families are suffering. In connection with the proposed monument, I had a rather bitter letter sent me from a woman in the West, whom I know very well.
I think I shall read it, because it reveals the feeling, not of the few, but of hundreds of re-

Supply-Public Works
turned men and of their wives. I have hundreds of them in my own constituency, and in this regard I speak for the returned men themselves This woman, whose husband was out of work, had to put her children away for a time in order that she might work and try to keep things going. The letter reads:
May I suggest that instead of spending money on the fallen, they spend the money for the clothing, feeding and sheltering of the men who had the great misfortune to return to Canada with their lives. It is no fault of theirs if they are not among the so-called "glorious dead". Had these men returned they would be in the same category as their living comrades-in the bread line and the recipients of old clothes (by appeals in the press), doles, poverty, Hastings Park, etc. Canada has already forgotten those men who served Canada for the profiteer, and saved poverty and misery for themselves. Yes, our children will remember when they see their fathers and brothers who did come back, sick, miserable and in want. We are told there is no money to provide decent constructive work. No, but they could find money for war and for the destruction of life, but nothing to conserve life.
Thinking people are tired of this hypocritical cant about the dead, let us attend to the living. We dress up the dead with cenotaphs, etc., and we refuse the living bread.
I am not accusing the government, in attempting to erect a monument, of forgetting the living, but I do say that until there can be fuller provision made for the living, we ought to hesitate about erecting a monument in marble. One other thing which I think ought to be said is this: that in commemorating the war there ought to be the utmost care exercised as to the character ol that commemoration. No man of this generation is likely to forget the Great War. It has touched too many of our homes. We are struggling beneath an enormous national debt because of this great war. The whole world to-day is upside down to a large extent because of the war, and I for one want to protest once more that, however we may accord the utmost sympathy to the men who risked their lives and the many who gave their lives at the front, we must be very careful lest in any sense whatever we glorify war or militarism. If there is any monument erected at all, whilst it might contain some tribute to the men who gave their lives, it also ought to point out that, after all, war is, from the beginning to the end, a miserable failure. The monument ought to commemorate the failure cf the war to obtain one of the slightest things for which we went to war. In saying this I speak not merely from the standpoint of a few individuals, but for a very large section of the working class, and, in addition to that, for a large section of the people of Canada, who as a rule [DOT]do not get their opinions before the public. I feel that I could not let this opportunity 171
pass without protesting against the erection of a monument of this kind.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am surprised at the remarks of my hon. friend from Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth). If he assumes the government has any desire to glorify war he is entirely mistaken. There is a great difference between glorifying war and glorifying patriotism or glorifying sacrifice, the greatest patriotism and the greatest sacrifice which the country has ever known. That is what the government seeks to glorify in the monument, and what I believe the nation hopes to see glorified. When my hon. friend speaks about caring for the poor and the hungry, I think it is not unfair to remind him of a reference or two that might appropriately be made at this time. There is a saying which my hon. friend will recall, to the effect that man does not live by bread alone.

Man cannot live
very well without bread.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No, and he
cannot live without the other. If it is a choice between living without bread and living without a spirit that is ready for sacrifice, I think the majority of men would prefer the spirit of sacrifice to bread. It is the spirit of heroism, the spirit of self-sacrifice, the spirit of all that is noble and great, that was exemplified in the lives of those sacrificed in the Great War, and the services rendered by the men and women who went overseas; and the nation will be dead the minute it loses that vision. It is that vision which the government wishes to keep alive in erecting a monument of this kind. Every point my hon. friend has urged might have been put forward by the Pharisee and his associates who rebuked the woman who broke the alabaster box of ointment over her Saviour. Why, they said, it was a waste. It was all thrown away. Its contents might have been sold and given to the poor. They were unable to appreciate the spirit of sacrifice and understanding that really accounts for all that is noblest and best by way of inspiration in the world. Everything in life is not to be measured by its mere utility value. There is a side of life loftier than that of the mere material satisfaction of daily physical needs. I do not think I need emphasize that point with my hon. friend. I think he appreciates it as well as any one, but what I am protesting against is his venturing to assert, in the name of labour or any group in the community, that the government should not seek to perpetuate in the minds of our own and future generations in this country the greatest service, the greatest

Supply-Public Works

sacrifice ever rendered by the nation in a cause which was the greatest the world has known in the history of human freedom.

I wish to dissociate myself, in any apparent criticism of this item, from the remarks of my hon. friend from Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woods-worth). He has spoken of the debt which we in Canada owe. It is a large sum we all know, but we are able to pay it. We owe a debt to the soldiers who have gone overseas and made the supreme sacrifice, and this is one way in which we are able to pay part of it, and one way which I hope, we will not overlook or neglect. My only object in asking the minister for information-and I sincerely hope the item will be carried-is to ensure that the most careful and thorough investigation will be made by the government, that suitable plans will be prepared and procured that this item will not be lost sight of in the pressure of the many other items and important business of this country. I quite agree with the remarks of the Prime Minister, and I sincerely hope that we will soon have erected a monument somewhat iD keeping with the sacifice and the service which our soldiers have given overseas.

I am very anxious to see eeonomy practised, but I could not oppose this motion. I believe, with the member for Centre Winnipeg, that it is wise that we should educate our people against war. Nevertheless, after they have made the sacrifices that were absolutely necessary during the recent Great War, I think it is well we should commemorate those sacrifices. With the hou. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Knox), I too would like very much if we could know at the present time more nearly what this monument, is going to cost, and if it would be possible to get plans without the expenditure of even the sum of $10,000. I do not know whether that is possible or not; but as has been said after $10,000 has been expended one feels, well, that we do not like to waste the $10,000, and even though the monument may cost a sum that we do not feel like expending just yet, that expenditure may be used as a leverage to go on. The necessity for money and for relief from the burden of taxation at the present time is at present very great, but I hope that, at least in a few years a monument will be erected to commemorate the great sacrifices of our soldiers at the front. As I said before, I am anxious for economy. In fact, while I have not criticized the expenditures that we have just passed at the instance of the Minister of Public Works, if I

had the opportunity of using the knife on them, I would cut out quite a goodly numbe-where expenditures are made on harbours for merely local traffic. When the case is one of through traffic, I can see the reasonableness of spending money from the Dominion treasury; but where it is only for local traffic, merely a local affiair, I cannot see any reason why it should not be left to the provinces or even to the towns and cities to construct their own harbours. As regards this appropriation if the plans cannot be secured for a less amount than that, I am willing to support it.

As regards another section of this item, the National Gallery of Canada, I notice that the expenditure has increased by 100 per cent, from $50,000 to $100,000. Can the minister explain what that increase means?
That appropriation was discussed and passed some time ago.
These items under "Miscellaneous" are all carried except the last one.
I thought the whole item No. 168 went together.
They are all passed except the last, the National monument.
I understand, however, that even when one item is left, we can discuss the others.

This matter was discussed at the time, and my hon. friend will find in Hansard of that date a full explanation why the additional amount was granted.
Mr. MaeLAREN: I quite undertsand, regarding the estimate for the National monument, that the amount should be indefinite: but I think any such sum as is mentioned, $50,000 or $75,000, will not in any way provide the memorial that the Canadian people would wish to have. I would suggest to the government that if delay is not material, when a monument is erected, it should be put up in accord with the ideals of our people, and that would involve a much larger sum than the one suggested. If a monument is to be erected, as I think one should be, it should be done on somewhat of a grand style.

I was very much interested in the remarks of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) as regards this question.
I was also interested in what was said by the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth). Perhaps there is a little confusion of mind between the Prime Minister

Supply-Public Works
and the hon. member for Winnipeg. I do not suppose that the latter meant to convey any idea that he was opposed to memorializing the heroism of our Canadian soldiers. I do not think anybody is opposed to that. But this is a matter worthy of much more thought than this House is giving to it, and, perhaps, worthy of more thought than the government has given to it so far. I am just wondering if to build a heap of stone is, after all, the best way of memorializing greatness. I think we shall all be willing to concede the great courage which the Canadian soldiers manifested, and we shall be willing to erect a monument, whether in stone or in some other form, that will express in the best possible way our appreciation of that courage. But if we are seeking to express our appreciation of heroism, would it not be well if it took a little heroism to do that? Can we not find a way of expressing our appreciation of the greatness and heroism of our soldiers that will take a little heroism on the part of legislatures and of Canada? For instance, could we not memorialize them with a statute or, if necessary, more than one statute that would give a shred of reflection of the liberty for which they ched, that would be an embodiment of a shadow of the ideal for which they poured out their blood? I do not object to your building a monument that will reach to the stars, if you will, and then it would not express their greatness. But surely there is something deeper, more beautiful, of greater utility tnan that, and that could be found, perhaps, in legislation, in such an alteration of the economic system under which their brothers are spared to live, under which their children will grow %up, that will be a nobler monument than a heap of marble or of rock. So I would suggest that before we hastily decide to follow precedent, to follow the ancient countries that have built their memorials to war, we would seek if haply, we might not find a better way of expressing our appreciation of the greatness of the Canadian soldiers who died in a way that was supposed to end all wars, and who died thinking to bring liberty and peace-and all such words that we have been so fond of mouthing.
One more thought. It looks a little incongruous that we should convert into marble or rock, actual material that seems to be needed by those who happen to have been spared from the great conflict. If we are going to beautify Canada, or Ottawa, or any other city, or any part of the world for that matter, as a means of expressing our respect for our dead, it might be well to wait until we
171i
can do that without suffering, if indeed we are so pinched as a nation. That, of course, I do not believe; I do not believe in this miserable prating about economy, and I am prepared to vote against economy of the kind that we have been talking about. But seeing that the government and the people and the House think so, then let us wait until we can do this without a man standing aside and wondering at a dead soldier getting more than a living one. I should like to see a memorial built when the living soldiers can say: "We are not suffering because of that." That is all I think my hon. friend from Centre Winnipeg meant to convey, and I would submit that as a thought to the government. There is no hurry. Perhaps this is not the best way of commemorating the dead; but when we do this, let us do it in the best possible way, and I do not know that this would be best expressed in a monument of rock.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: May I say to my hon. friend that I doubt very much whether he or the hon. member to whom he has alluded would have the privilege of speaking in this House to-night the words of liberty which they are professing to utter, but for the sacrifices of the men whose heroism the government is seeking to commemorate in this simple way? The least the nation can do is to erect in its capital some memorial that will be worthy, in its appearance, in its symbolism, in the greatness of its noble position, structure, proportion and beauty, of the spirit that was exemplified in that great sacrifice. My hon. friend has referred to labour. Where do all the great works of art come from? They have been for the most part contributed by those who, bom amid humble surroundings through years of struggle and toil, assisted here and there by such bits of inspiration and aid as the nation could give them, have come through their art to be numbered among the country's greatest. When a nation loses what is signified by its art it loses its own spirit, and when it loses the remembrance of the sacrifices and heroism by which it has gained the liberty it enjoys, it loses all the vision that makes a people great.

I do not want to take up too much of the time of the committee, but I do not wish the implication of the Prime Minister to go unchallenged. There was nothing in what I said that would not express just as much gratitude to the soldiers of Canada as the Prime Minister has expressed; neither have I suggested that we should not build a monument. That is not the point.

Supply-Public Works
The question I raised was whether the proposed monument was the best form in which we could express our gratitude to the soldiers; and in the second place I wondered whether we could not undertake this work at a time when we were economically in a better position to do so. I still think that this perhaps is not the best way, and also that there are other things more necessary to be done at this time. So that in my view it would be well for us to wait a little longer in order that we might carry out in a much better way what is now intended. That is all I said and it is not necessary to throw out the suggestion that anyone is failing to appreciate the sacrifices of the Canadian soldiers.

Item agreed to.
Public buildings-Quebec-Terrebonne-New public building (Governor General's warrant, December 19, 1922), $26,000.

During the recent unfortunate fire in this community the Dominion public building was destroyed. A desire was expressed by the citizens that the building should be immediately restored, and owing to the fact that a great many of the people in the community belong to the labouring class it was suggested that it would be of greater advantage to them if the restoration could be undertaken almost at once in order to provide labour for those who had suffered so severely from the fire. The government asked for the Governor General's warrant to undertake the work, and this vote is to confirm the warrant.
What is the character of the building?
It is a post office and customs building.
What is the total cost of the building?

I understood the minister's reason for the warrant to be that there were certain persons out of work because of the fire. I do not object to the building being restored, but what was the reason for the warrant?

A public building was suddenly destroyed by fire and there was no way of providing money for its restoration except either to wait until parliament met or to ask for the Governor General's warrant The latter course was followed. My explanation I think is a fair one. The town of Terrebonne is composed largely of labouring people

and after the fire many of them who had lost their properties were in distress.
The fire, then, extended beyond the public building?
Yes, practically the whole town was burnt.
Oh, that is different.
It was felt that some measure of relief could be given by undertaking the immediate restoration of the public building.
That explains the matter, and it seems to be the proper thing to do.

Legislation-House of Commons-salaries (including H. P. Arsenault as Chief Translator-Bluebooks-at an initial salary of $3,480, from 1 April, 1923, notwithstanding anything to the contrary in the Civil Service Act or amendments thereto), $236,545.

In explanation of this item, Mr. Chairman, I may say that the staff of translators was short of two or three men last year, and as Mr. Desaulniers, was chief of the Blue Books branch, was superannuated, the question came up of replacing him. There were several men competent for the position, but I had to make a choice which would justify itself not only on the point of professional ability, but also on the point of discipline and administration, and out of the several candidates who were mentioned the name of Mr. Arsenault seemed to me to be the one which would be best favoured by the staff because of his administrative ability and official authority. He is not a newcomer, he has been ten years on the staff. I may say that those who were competitors for the position were agreeable to his election.
Have we not divided the staff into two p&rts really, and put Mr. Arsenault in charge of one part and someone else in charge of the other?

We have abolished the position of assistant chief. We have appointed Mr. Arsenault as chief of the Blue Books and Mr. Paradis as chief of the Law Branch translation. They are two very important positions because the reports are read in Europe not only in France but in other countries where the French language is most familiar, and consequently we must have excellent translations.
Why is it necessary to name the official? Does it not come under the Civil Service Act ordinarily, and is not this an appointment outside of the provisions of . the act?

Yes, and no. The Civil
Service Commission have an examination, of course, but all these appointments would have to come before the committee anyway, because the organization of its staff is under the purview of the House of Commons. But when the competition took place before the
Civil Service Commission there were, I think, three or four candidates, of whom two were most prominent, Mr. Arsenault and Mr. Keliher? Mr. Keliher himelf came to see me at the time and said he preferred to be in the Hansard branch where we had a vacancy. So we appointed Mr. Arsenault. But as the commission declared that Mr. Keliher should be in Mr. Arsenault's place, we had to come before the committee and word the item as it appears in the estimates.
In view of Mr. Keliher's attitude towards the question, could not the commission have changed their nomination?

That is what I intended, but it was done during my absence in Europe, and I found the estimates as they are. At all events, I would have to come before the committee with the name of Mr. Arsenault in the estimates.
I understand Mr. Keliher is quite agreeable?
Yes, he came to see me and said he was quite willing to go to the Hansard branch.
Does anyone feel that he has been passed over?
No.
The reason I ask is that I heard from some source, I cannot remember which at the moment, that there was some disappointment in relation to the appointment.
Oh, no.

As the restaurant is supplied with space, light, heat, furnishing and equipment of all kinds free, it should not cost the country such a large sum as this. I believe that someone has figured it out at about $100 for each person who is entitled to use the restaurant. If the charge for meals is too low, it should be increased. I cannot think we are justified before the country in putting on it a heavy account like this for what is after all simply a convenience for members.

The restaurant is under the direction of a joint committee of the House of Commons and Senate. It so happens that we had a meeting at the beginning of the week. This salary of the manager of the restaurant was fixed at the meeting which was held during last session. It is a committee which has been in existence since confederation, and I may say as an old member -in fact, looking around me, as the oldest member of the House-that in all my parliamentary life we have never had a restaurant which gave more satisfaction than the present one. It must be borne in mind that not only the members but their wives share in the benefits afforded by the restaurant, and that we must have a man there who is familiar with restaurant management. We are very fortunate in having Mr. George. I am sure if he were manager of the Chateau Laurier, here, or the Ritz Carlton in Montreal, or any other large hotel, he would receive a much larger salary than that which is paid to him as manager of our restaurant. I have this to say for Mr. George: he came here, I think, as a page; he has been here thirty-five or,forty years, and as we say in common parlance, he "knows the ropes." He is diligent; he is sober-naturally; he is very intelligent, and 
gives excellent service. As I have said, this increased salary has been fixed by the joint commitijee on the restaurant, comprising members of both Houses. If my horn friend will think of what is paid to managers of large hotels and even to restaurants in cities and towns, he will realize that this amount is not excessive.

I am not objecting
to the manager's salary in any sense whatever; I have been quite misunderstood. I see in the estimate one item for the manager's salary, $2,520; maintenance, $20,000; and, in the supplementary estimates, a further sum of $7,500. That is a total of $30,000 for the maintenance of this institution. I do not criticize the salary of the manager; I presume it is none too high. I am not criticising in any sense the service rendered by the restaurant. But it does seem to me that from the standpoint of the public at large, $30,000 is a very large sum to pay over and above the granting of a room with free light, heat and equipment. I doubt whether we are justified in asking the public to put up that $30,000, which after all, we know must be paid from the taxes of the people.

It must be remembered
that in the carrying on of the restaurant we must have a personnel which is not employed the whole year round, and my hon. friend knows that you cannot get servants, domestics, as cheaply to-day as you could some years ago. The food is excellent; there has been no complaint in that respect. Of course it costs a little money, but it is a matter that is in the hands of the legislators. If it is the desire to abolish the restaurant, hon. members have only to say so, but as long as we maintain it for the members, the senators and the principal employees, we must expect to have to pay something. But I made an examination of the accounts the other day, and I am pleased to be able to say that for the first time we shall be able out of the profits-because the restaurant is now a profit-making institution-to apply something in abatement of the expenditure involved in maintenance. So that if under Mr. George the restaurant continues to be well managed, I am sure my hon. friend will next year find that figure for maintenance much decreased.

I have no objection to the resolution carrying, but I have been impressed, as one who has now got to be a pretty old member of the House, by the fact that there is a great deal of money wasted in the library. Although I use it about as much as the average member, if not more-
I am sorry to say, not as much in recent years as formerly-I am sure there is a great deal of stuff bought for the library that I do not think anyone sees from one year's end to the other. I think it would be well to bring home to the librarians the wisdom of revising the whole purchase programme to see if economies could not be effected by curtailing some of the things for which we now vote very considerable sums. The library also is getting cluttered up, and there is scarcely room to get around. I know it has been rearranged lately and very much improved in that respect, but I would think that something should be done to
11 p.m. bring the reading matter that is in the library more in conformity with the actual needs of members of parliament. It seems to me it now spreads into too large a field and that much that is there is not worth the room it occupies.

The right hon. gentleman is quite right. Last year there was a meeting of the joint committee on the Library of Parliament, which is composed, as in the case of the restaurant committee, of members of both houses, and on that occasion we decided to remove to the Archives building many of the files of old papers that were accumulating in the library. I agree that a better choice of books might be made. The trouble with the library is that it is at present in a transient stage. As the right hon. gentleman knows, when the construction of this building was decided upon, plans were made to extend the library, but in view of the extra cost involved it was decided to postpone these suggested changes. The result is that many valuable books were never seen on the shelves but are stored away below the Senate lobby and in an area extending nearly up to our portion of the building. The purchase of books, reviews, encyclopaedias, etc., might be a little more judicious than it has been. The librarian of to-day, or to express myself more correctly the up-to-date librarian, differs totally from the librarian of yesterday. To-day the conduct of the library amounts to a science. The library of congress at Washington is a magnificient library. They have there probably the most elaborate organization I have seen in that regard. Over there the management of libraries has developed into a science
and in the universities lectures have been given on the art of becoming an efficient librarian. So far we have not enjoyed that advantage in Canada but our institutions of this character are developing. We now possess libraries, thanks to the munificence of Carnegie and other benefactors of humanity. For the future I believe we certainly ought to adopt the views of the right hon. gentleman and see to it that our parliamentary library is especially adapted to the needs of parliament.

I ain glad that the Speaker has called attention to the modem scientific libraries. It would appear that with the immense amount that is being spent on our library, and with the large number of books we already possess, there ought to be some better arrangement for caring for them than exists at present. I fhink anyone who knows anything about libraries will recognize there is a handicap our librarians suffer from that cannot very well be overcome. I refer to the lack of stock room. Undoubtedly that is a very great inconvenience. The books are packed into a space that is really not sufficient for more than a quarter of their number. Not only is the arrangement bad, but the structure is far from being modern. I wonder sometimes whether, until such times as we have a suitable library building, the library could not be departmentalized and certain sections of it placed in other parts of the building, making it more available than it is to-day. Further, I should like to suggest that although the librarians are kindness itself we ought to have some more modem system of indexing and cataloguing than prevails at the present time.
The hon. the Speaker has referred to the congressional library. At Washington, they have worked out a system of cataloguing and indexing that might be very well applied to our library here. The system is being adopted in many small libraries throughout the country and is proving a very great convenience to anyone wanting to consult the institution. Further than that, it would be a very great advantage to all the members if some system were adopted for filing clippings, magazine articles and legislative material dealing particularly with topics that concern us in parliament,. I remember a few years ago visiting the state library in Wisconsin where Mr. Charles McCarthy, who was rather a genius and tremendously interested in this work, had evolved a veiy valuable scheme for making available to all the members of the state legislature the information that existed
